analysis.headline: Introduced with the backing of 9 Republican senators, the Fair Tax Act never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy, starting in 2013. It would abolish the IRS after 2015 and have states collect the tax instead. Families could register to get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. Purchases made for business, investment, or export purposes would not be taxed at all.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: the income tax on their wages, capital gains, and dividends disappears, the estate and gift tax on large inheritances disappears, and because purchases made for investment purposes are exempt, returns on wealth largely escape taxation. Businesses gain from untaxed business and investment purchases and from the repeal of payroll taxes. Low-income families get the rebate, which offsets the sales tax up to the poverty line, and everyone stops filing income-tax returns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes entirely.
Imposes a 23% national sales tax in 2013, with the rate subject to adjustment in later years.
Exempts all purchases made for business, investment, or export purposes, so returns on savings and assets are not taxed.
Provides a monthly rebate to registered families equal to the sales tax on poverty-level spending.
Prohibits funding of the IRS after fiscal year 2015 and has states, rather than the federal government, collect the tax in exchange for a small administration fee.

analysis.who_pays: Middle-income households who spend most of what they earn would pay the 23% tax on nearly every purchase — groceries, cars, rent-related services, health care, new homes — while the tax they currently pay on wages would be gone. Any household spending above the rebate's poverty-level floor pays more tax on consumption than high savers do, because income that is saved and invested is never taxed. Social Security and Medicare would be funded from general sales tax revenue instead of dedicated payroll taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households spending most of their income

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax falls hardest on families who spend most of their income, while purchases made for investment purposes are exempt, so income earned from wealth goes untaxed under the bill's terms.
The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes, which apply only to the largest inheritances.
The 23% rate applies only in 2013; after that the rate is a formula that can be adjusted upward, so the final rate is not locked in.

The rebate is not automatic: families must register annually with Social Security numbers and certify lawful residency and household membership, and a family that fails to register loses its rebate payments after a grace period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real appeal — no income-tax filing, no IRS, and a rebate that shields the poorest families from the sales tax — is genuine, and the bill's text does deliver those things. But the core trade is structural: it moves taxation away from income and wealth (including large inheritances and investment returns, which would go untaxed) and onto consumption, which takes a larger share of a middle- or working-class household's budget than of a wealthy one's. The rebate softens but does not eliminate that shift, and the adjustable post-2013 rate means the true long-run burden is not fixed by the bill's headline number.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Saxby Chambliss introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2011 in the Senate on January 25, 2011, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Isakson, Moran, Burr, Coburn, and DeMint.
Eight senators cosponsored the bill, all Republicans.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the 112th Congress.

The bill would have repealed income, payroll, and estate taxes, imposed a 23% national sales tax, defunded the IRS after 2015, and terminated the sales tax if the Sixteenth Amendment were not repealed within seven years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so no one gained a windfall — but because the bill died quietly in committee, the existing tax code stayed in place, and the high-income households and large estates that would have benefited from repealing the income and estate taxes never got that benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code stayed in place

for.name: Saxby Chambliss
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill's lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2011 in the Senate on January 25, 2011.

for.name: Americans for Fair Taxation
for.role: Advocacy organization promoting the FairTax plan
for.what_they_did: Long-running national advocacy campaign for a national sales tax to replace the income tax; the bill carries its proposal.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action for two years.

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators behind the bill were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee never took it up.

industries.note: The bill repeals the taxes that fall most heavily on them — income tax on capital gains and dividends, and the estate and gift tax — while exempting investment purchases from the sales tax. The offsetting cost falls on consumption, which weighs heaviest on households spending most of their income.

With the income tax repealed and purchases for investment purposes exempt, returns on capital would be untaxed, and financial intermediation services would be taxed only through a narrow fee-based mechanism.

Sellers take on the duty to collect and remit the tax, with segregation accounts, reporting, and penalties for failure, but the bill pays them an administration credit of at least $200 or a quarter of one percent of tax remitted, and repeals the income and payroll taxes on their businesses.
States with existing sales taxes become the primary collectors of the federal tax, locking them into a federal revenue role in exchange for a small administration fee.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS eliminates the annual filing business the industry depends on, though sales-tax compliance work would partly replace it.
